title: Why QLoRA's 2e-4 Default Learning Rate Overfits Small Datasets
hook: Every QLoRA tutorial says start at 2e-4. That number comes from Alpaca's 52k samples — and on the 5-10k-sample datasets most people actually fine-tune on, it can overfit before epoch one ends.
key_points: The ubiquitous QLoRA learning-rate default of 2e-4 traces back to the Alpaca paper's 52k-sample fine-tuning run.
On smaller, self-collected datasets (roughly under 10k samples), that rate can push the model to overfit within the first epoch.
Symptom: training loss keeps falling smoothly while eval loss stalls or climbs — a classic overfitting signature, not a data-quality bug.
The poster spent weeks re-cleaning data and rewriting prompt templates before suspecting the learning rate itself.
content_html: A widely-shared Reddit post argues that one of the most copy-pasted numbers in fine-tuning — QLoRA's 2e-4 learning rate — is quietly wrong for a lot of use cases. Every tutorial, from Unsloth's docs to Hugging Face examples to the original paper, uses it. But that number was tuned on Alpaca's 52,000-sample dataset, and most practitioners are fine-tuning on datasets they scraped and labeled themselves — often 5,000 to 10,000 samples.
extra_html: At that smaller scale, the poster found the model overfitting inside the first epoch: training loss looked great while eval loss sat flat or climbed. They describe burning close to three weeks chasing the wrong culprits — re-cleaning the dataset twice, rewriting the prompt template twice — before landing on the learning rate itself as the likely cause. The practical takeaway for anyone fine-tuning on a small custom dataset: don't treat 2e-4 as gospel, and treat overfitting inside epoch one as a hyperparameter signal rather than a data problem. Posted to r/MachineLearning, July 2026 — see the thread for the original writeup.

related.title: QLoRA: Fine-tuning Quantized LLMs
related.hook: Fine-tune a model with tens of billions of parameters on a single GPU. QLoRA squeezes the frozen base to 4-bit, then trains LoRA adapters on top — without losing quality.

related.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
related.hook: Why retrain billions of weights when you can freeze them all and train tiny add-on matrices instead? LoRA tunes under ~1% of the parameters with near-full-fine-tune quality.

related.title: Learning Rate & Schedules
related.hook: The single most important hyperparameter: set it too high and training diverges, too low and it crawls — so we warm it up, then decay it.

flashcards.prompt: Where does the widely-copied QLoRA default learning rate of 2e-4 actually come from?
flashcards.back_html: It comes from the Alpaca paper's fine-tuning run on 52,000 samples — a dataset size much larger than most custom fine-tuning jobs.

flashcards.prompt: What's the telltale sign that the 2e-4 rate is too high for your small dataset?

choices.text: Training loss keeps dropping smoothly while eval loss stalls or rises
Training loss oscillates wildly and never decreases
The model refuses to produce any output at all

flashcards.explanation_html: That pattern — smooth training loss, flat or worsening eval loss — is the classic signature of overfitting, which is what happens when a too-high learning rate memorizes a small dataset fast.

flashcards.prompt: Roughly what dataset size does the poster flag as the danger zone for the 2e-4 default?
flashcards.explanation_html: 52k-sample Alpaca is where 2e-4 was tuned; the poster argues datasets well below 10k samples overfit at that rate because there's so much less data to absorb the same step size.
